{{short description|Method of estimating statistical parameters}}

In [[probability theory]] and [[statistics]],  '''empirical likelihood''' ('''EL''') is a nonparametric method for estimating the parameters of [[statistical models]]. It requires fewer assumptions about the [[error distribution]] while retaining some of the merits in [[Likelihood function|likelihood]]-based inference. The estimation method requires that the data are [[Independent and identically distributed random variables|independent and identically distributed]] (iid). It performs well even when the distribution is [[Skewness|asymmetric]] or [[Censoring (statistics)|censored]].<ref>{{Cite book|last=Owen|first=Art B.|title=Empirical likelihood|date=2001|isbn=978-1-4200-3615-2|location=Boca Raton, Fla.|oclc=71012491}}</ref> EL methods can also handle constraints and prior information on parameters. [[Art Owen]] pioneered work in this area with his 1988 paper.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Owen|first=Art B.|date=1988|title=Empirical likelihood ratio confidence intervals for a single functional|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1093/biomet/75.2.237|journal=Biometrika|volume=75|issue=2|pages=237–249|doi=10.1093/biomet/75.2.237|issn=0006-3444|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

== Definition ==
Given a set of <math>n</math> i.i.d. realizations <math>y_i</math> of random variables <math>Y_i</math>, then the [[empirical distribution function]] is <math>\hat{F}(y):=\sum_{i=1}^n \pi_i I(Y_i<y)</math>, with the indicator function <math>I</math> and the (normalized) weights <math>\pi_i</math>.
Then, the empirical likelihood is:<ref><math>\frac{\hat{F}(y_i)-\hat{F}(y_i-\delta y)}{\delta y}</math> is an estimate of the probability density, compare [[histogram]]</ref>
:<math>L:=\prod_{i=1}^n \frac{\hat{F}(y_i)-\hat{F}(y_i-\delta y)}{\delta y},</math>
where <math>\delta y</math> is a small number (potentially the difference to the next smaller sample).

Empirical likelihood estimation can be augmented with side information by using further constraints (similar to the [[generalized estimating equations]] approach) for the empirical distribution function. 
E.g. a constraint like the following can be incorporated using a Lagrange multiplier <math>E[h(Y;\theta)]=\int_{-\infty}^\infty h(y;\theta) dF=0</math> which implies <math>\hat{E}[h(y;\theta)]=\sum_{i=1}^n h(y_i;\theta)\pi_i=0</math>.

With similar constraints, we could also model correlation.

=== Discrete random variables ===
The empirical-likelihood method can also be also employed for [[discrete distribution]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Wang|first1=Dong|last2=Chen|first2=Song Xi|date=2009-02-01|title=Empirical likelihood for estimating equations with missing values|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1214/07-aos585|journal=The Annals of Statistics|volume=37|issue=1|doi=10.1214/07-aos585|s2cid=5427751 |issn=0090-5364|arxiv=0903.0726}}</ref>
Given <math>\ p_{i}:=\hat{F}(y_i)-\hat{F}(y_i-\delta y),\ i = 1,...,n </math> such that 
<math>p_i \geq 0 \text{ and } \sum_{i=1}^n\ p_{i} =1.</math>

Then the empirical likelihood is again <math>L(p_{1},...,p_{n})= \prod_{i=1}^n \ p_{i}</math>.

Using the [[Lagrangian multiplier]] method to maximize the [[logarithm]] of the empirical likelihood subject to the trivial normalization constraint, we find <math>p_i = 1/n</math> as a maximum. Therefore, <math>\hat{F}</math> is the [[empirical distribution function]].

==Estimation Procedure==
EL estimates are calculated by maximizing the empirical [[likelihood function]] (see above) subject to constraints based on the [[estimating function]] and the trivial assumption that the probability weights of the likelihood function sum to 1.<ref>Mittelhammer, Judge, and Miller (2000), 292.</ref> This procedure is represented as:
: <math>
    \max_{\pi_{i}, \theta} \ln(L)=
    \max_{\pi_{i}, \theta} \sum_{i=1}^n \ln \pi_i 
  </math>
subject to the constraints
:<math>
     s.t. \sum_{i=1}^n\pi_i = 1, \sum_{i=1}^n\pi_i h(y_i;\theta) = 0,\forall i\in[1..n]\quad 0\le\pi_i.
 </math><ref name="Bera2002">{{cite journal |last1=Bera |first1=Anil K. |last2=Bilias |first2=Yannis |title=The MM, ME, ML, EL, EF and GMM approaches to estimation: a synthesis |journal=Journal of Econometrics |date=2002 |volume=107 |issue=1–2 |pages=51–86 |doi=10.1016/S0304-4076(01)00113-0}}</ref>{{rp|at=Equation (73)}}

The value of the theta parameter can be found by solving the [[Lagrange multiplier|Lagrangian function]]
:<math>
  \mathcal{L} = \sum_{i=1}^n \ln \pi_{i} + \mu (1- \sum_{i=1}^n \pi_{i})-n\tau' \sum_{i=1}^n \pi_{i} h(y_{i};\theta).
</math><ref name="Bera2002" />{{rp|at=Equation (74)}}

There is a clear analogy between this maximization problem and the one solved for [[Maximum entropy probability distribution#Proof|maximum entropy]].

The parameters <math>\pi_i</math> are [[nuisance parameter]]s.

== Empirical Likelihood Ratio (ELR) ==
An empirical likelihood ratio function is defined and used to obtain confidence intervals parameter of interest θ similar to parametric likelihood ratio confidence intervals.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Owen|first=Art|date=1990-03-01|title=Empirical Likelihood Ratio Confidence Regions|journal=The Annals of Statistics|volume=18|issue=1|doi=10.1214/aos/1176347494|issn=0090-5364|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Dong|first1=Lauren Bin|last2=Giles|first2=David E. A.|date=2007-01-30|title=An Empirical Likelihood Ratio Test for Normality|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/03610910601096544|journal=Communications in Statistics - Simulation and Computation|volume=36|issue=1|pages=197–215|doi=10.1080/03610910601096544|s2cid=16866055 |issn=0361-0918|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Let L(F) be the empirical likelihood of function <math>F</math>, then the ELR would be:

<math>R(F)=L(F)/L(F_{n})</math>.

Consider sets of the form

<math>C = \{ T(F)| R(F) \geq r \}</math>.

Under such conditions a test of <math>T(F)=t</math> rejects when t does not belong to <math>C</math>, that is, when no distribution F with <math>T(F)=t</math> has likelihood <math>L(F) \geq rL(F_{n})</math>.

The central result is for the mean of X. Clearly, some restrictions on <math>F</math> are needed, or else <math>C = \reals^p</math> whenever <math>r < 1</math>. To see this, let:

<math>F = \epsilon \delta_{x} + (1- \epsilon) F_{n}</math>

If <math>\epsilon</math> is small enough and  <math>\epsilon >0</math>, then <math>R(F) \geq r</math>.

But then, as <math>x</math> ranges through <math>\reals^p</math>, so does the mean of <math>F</math>, tracing out <math>C = \reals^p</math>. The problem can be solved by restricting to distributions F that are supported in a bounded set. It turns out to be possible to restrict attention t distributions with support in the sample, in other words, to distribution <math>F \ll F_{n}</math>. Such method is convenient since the statistician might not be willing to specify a bounded support for <math>F</math>, and since <math>t</math> converts the construction of <math>C</math> into a finite dimensional problem.

== Other Applications ==
The use of empirical likelihood is not limited to confidence intervals. In efficient [[quantile regression]], an EL-based categorization<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Chen|first1=Jien|last2=Lazar|first2=Nicole A.|date=2010-01-27|title=Quantile estimation for discrete data via empirical likelihood|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/10485250903301525|journal=Journal of Nonparametric Statistics|volume=22|issue=2|pages=237–255|doi=10.1080/10485250903301525|s2cid=119684596 |issn=1048-5252|url-access=subscription}}</ref> procedure helps determine the shape of the true discrete distribution at level p, and also provides a way of formulating a [[consistent estimator]]. In addition, EL can be used in place of parametric likelihood to form [[model selection]] criteria.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Chen|first1=Chixiang|last2=Wang|first2=Ming|last3=Wu|first3=Rongling|last4=Li|first4=Runze|date=2022|title=A Robust Consistent Information Criterion for Model Selection Based on Empirical Likelihood|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.5705/ss.202020.0254|journal=Statistica Sinica|doi=10.5705/ss.202020.0254|doi-broken-date=12 July 2025 |arxiv=2006.13281 |s2cid=220042083 |issn=1017-0405}}</ref>
Empirical likelihood can naturally be applied in [[survival analysis]]<ref>Zhou, M. (2015). Empirical Likelihood Method in Survival Analysis (1st ed.). Chapman and Hall/CRC. https://doi.org/10.1201/b18598</ref> or regression problems<ref>Chen, Song Xi, and Ingrid Van Keilegom. "A review on empirical likelihood methods for regression." TEST volume 18, pages 415–447, (2009) https://doi.org/10.1007/s11749-009-0159-5</ref>
